title: Virginia university report finds officials did not disclose student’s terror conviction
description: An ODU report says federal officials never alerted the university that a returning student had been convicted of supporting ISIS before the deadly ROTC classroom shooting.
fullText:
An independent investigation into the deadly March terror attack at Old Dominion University (ODU) found that federal officials never warned the school that the returning student behind the shooting had previously been convicted of trying to support ISIS.

On March 12, Mohamed Bailor Jalloh reportedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire inside an ROTC classroom at ODU, killing an Army veteran instructor and injuring two students before ROTC members fatally subdued him.

Jalloh was convicted in 2016 of attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State terror group in a plot to target U.S. military personnel.

Neither his federal probation officer, the Fbi, nor any state or federal agency notified ODU of his conviction, the university-commissioned report concluded.

Virginia Man Charged With Selling Weapon Used By Old Dominion University Gunman

"Had ODU known about Jalloh's criminal history, it is highly likely that ODU would have sought his removal from campus due to the risk he posed, particularly to military-affiliated individuals," the independent report said.

The FBI told Fox News Digital Thursday it is not the agency responsible for notifying colleges.

"The FBI does not serve as a notification authority for colleges or universities regarding an individual's criminal history – that is a shared responsibility across state, local, federal and community partners," the FBI said.

Additionally, the bureau noted that Jalloh's terrorism-related convictions were widely publicized by the Department of Justice in 2016 and 2017, with at least three press releases detailing his case still available on the agency's website.

"Furthermore, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia issued several press releases and publicly available information, including a press release when Jalloh was sentenced in 2017 for attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization," the agency said.

"The release remains on the Department of Justice website and can be found through an internet search with multiple links available."

Old Dominion University Shooter Identified As Mohamed Jalloh, Former National Guard Member, Isis Supporter

ODU said that, under Virginia law enacted in 2022, public universities are prohibited from asking applicants about their criminal history during the admissions process.

In compliance with the law, ODU said it removed criminal history questions from its applications, leaving the university dependent on voluntary student disclosures or outside law enforcement notifications.

Under Jalloh's federal supervised release, his probation officer reportedly had the authority to require him to disclose his criminal record to third parties.

However, no such notification was provided to any university office or campus police, according to the report.

"Given that Virginia law requires universities to rely on student self-disclosure, it is even more important that other law enforcement agencies ensure that information that universities need to know to safeguard their students is shared with universities. This critical failure led to tragic consequences here," the ODU report said.

Jalloh also never voluntarily disclosed his 2016 federal terrorism conviction to ODU, according to the report.

While Virginia law allows public universities to inquire about criminal history after an applicant is admitted, ODU's policy at the time only sent post-admission background questionnaires to first-time students, excluding readmitted returning students such as Jalloh.

According to the campus report, Jalloh first enrolled at ODU as an undergraduate student in 2007. After being academically suspended in 2010, he was readmitted in 2011 after serving in the Army National Guard.

He briefly took classes through spring 2012 before stopping for unknown reasons and was later convicted on federal terrorism charges in 2016.

He then served eight years in prison before being released in December 2024. Afterward, Jalloh applied for readmission as a returning student and was re-enrolled at ODU in 2025.

After Jalloh's case exposed a gap in the university's post-admission screening policies, ODU said it officially expanded its post-admission criminal history questionnaire to include readmitted students alongside first-time students.

Additionally, the report said nothing else on Jalloh's readmission application raised any concerns.

Jalloh's application reportedly listed a private residential address in Sterling, Virginia, rather than a federal prison address. Two professors who taught him in the months before the attack also reported no behavioral concerns.

The United States Probation and Pretrial Services Eastern District of Virginia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: The phone call that made Briton an NFL trailblazer
description: Seydou Traore is the first graduate of the UK-based NFL Academy to be drafted in the NFL. This is how he beat the odds.
fullText:
Seydou Traore has been waiting four hours for the phone call that will change his life. When it comes, he is the picture of calm. Next to him, his mum Zaia is anything but.

Traore and his family are sitting backstage at the NFL Draft, where the 23-year-old Briton - who did not see his loved ones for five years after moving to the US to try to become an NFL player - has just been told his dream is coming true.

Zaia, who is French-Algerian, lets out a 'zaghrouta' - a celebratory trilling sound that is traditional in north Africa - sheds tears of joy and has an out-of-body experience in a reaction that goes viral.

"I was in a trance," she tells BBC Sport. "I was like 'oh my God, it's happening, he's done it'. That's what I kept telling myself. It was pride and relief because it's been years, and it was all worth it."

Of all the social media content around Seydou's achievement in being the first graduate of England's NFL Academy to complete his pathway to the NFL, it is the clip of his mum he keeps watching.

He knows that she knows exactly what it has taken to defy the odds and become an NFL trailblazer.

A pep talk from the great Travis Kelce was just a tiny part.

Born and raised in south London, Traore was naturally athletic and tried many sports. He was playing football as a goalkeeper when he found American football at 16 with London Warriors.

In 2019 he earned a place in the first intake at the NFL Academy, a development programme initially based in north London and now in Loughborough. The academy recruits from many sport backgrounds and American football experience is not necessary.

Almost all draft prospects come through the American college system, which is why the academy was designed to help international players earn scholarships and prepare them for the NFL, mentally and physically.

Each year about one million teenagers play American football at high school in the US. About 0.08% of them reach the NFL.

One can therefore imagine how the odds are stacked against an international player like Traore.

But he applied himself to his dream, getting up at 5am and working all day every day to get better, either at the academy or training.

And the following summer, he had a breakthrough.

Traore's mum was in the kitchen when he came in and told her: "Some Americans want to speak with you. I've been talking to them for a while and, basically, I'm going to America."

Unknown to Zaia, her son had secured a spot at Florida high school Clearwater Academy. She told him: "I can't afford to come and see you, you'll be there by yourself."

For Traore's sister Zeinab, four years his senior, the thought of him moving 4,500 miles from home was even more difficult.

"He's like my first child so I'm protective," she says. "I was concerned at first. I thought it was too big a jump because he was still young."

Traore had been laying the foundations for this move for some time, making videos to showcase his skills.

One of them found its way to Clearwater head coach Jesse Chinchar.

"Wow, who's that?" Chinchar wondered as he watched a 6ft 3in guy leaping in the air to make a one-handed catch.

Little did he know that he was watching a Londoner who was yet to play a full-sided game of American football. But Clearwater had a track record of recruiting international players and helping them earn college scholarships.

"I did a bit more digging but there was no game film, just clips of him doing athletic stuff," says Chinchar.

"We got talking to Seydou and it felt like he was going to compete and wanted it for all the right reasons. You could tell how much it meant to him.

"It was kind of a wild adventure because he was one of the most raw, unknown commodities we had brought in, but we thought 'if this kid comes over and it works out, this could change his life'."

From day one Chinchar thought "we got something".

Traore learned his first playbook in a matter of days, which is like learning a new language. And playing as a wide receiver, he was immediately dominant against kids who had played the game their whole life.

He thinks his goalkeeping skills helped.

"Hand-eye coordination, tracking and locating balls, leaping down low or up high, and attacking the ball at corner kicks, that translates very well," Traore says.

"That's how American football is when they throw the ball up to you, you attack it at its highest point."

Chinchar agrees, adding: "I've felt that my guys who had a background in soccer have that understanding of spatial awareness, which I think in [American] football is an under-rated trait."

Chinchar was also impressed by Traore's character and self-belief. Even when he received his first college offer, he bet on himself getting a better one. That eventually came from Arkansas State.

Their head coach Butch Jones was working late when his tight ends coach came into his office and said: "I keep hearing about this player. I think he's special, there's something different about him."

They watched videos of Traore and Jones soon made a "hefty comparison". He called Seydou a clone of Travis Kelce, whom he coached at Cincinnati and helped convert into one of the best tight ends in NFL history.

"Seydou's size and stature coupled with his athleticism - the way he ran, the way he caught the ball – it made him a rare commodity," says Jones. "He had unlimited potential."

Traore had barely played at tight end and had already committed to another college. Jones therefore had to 'flip' him - so he called on his old friend.

He set up a group video call in which Kelce gave Seydou some advice and convinced him to trust coach Jones and his staff. Seydou signed in February 2021 and transitioned to tight end, showing natural instincts for the position.

Traore saw himself as a "big ball of clay" that Jones could mould, and the coach says he was "like a sponge" in terms of retaining information.

"In his first year Seydou looked like a young deer that could run but hadn't really matured yet, grown into his body," adds Jones.

"By year two you could see that development. He made some plays where you were in awe on the sideline."

Like Kelce, Traore can hurdle defenders, and in 2022 he was named the best tight end in the Sun Belt Conference. But he was determined to step up to the top level of college football and play in one of the Power Four conferences.

Seydou spent early 2023 with Colorado, whose tight ends coach called him out during a news conference, questioning his "toughness" and work ethic.

"We talked a few times when he was at Colorado, going through some tough times," says Jones.

"There was a lot of adversity through his journey, but he never gave up. He had that mental disposition it takes, every single day, to fight off the doubt that can creep in, especially when you're away from home."

In those moments, Seydou thought about his family.

"Knowing what I'd left and what I was trying to become was very motivating," he says.

After a term at Colorado, Seydou felt it best for his development to move on and he went to Mississippi State, who play in college football's most prestigious conference, the Southeastern.

But because he had transferred twice in quick succession, NCAA rules meant he could not play during 2023. All he could do was train.

It was then that Seydou found out just how much he wanted it. He treated it as a chance to improve his game, and when he finally played for Mississippi State in 2024, he was one of their top receiving threats.

Then in 2025, he began to catch the eye of NFL scouts. He scored a career-high five touchdowns and became a fans' favourite for his new tea-sipping celebration, a nod to the British stereotype.

Seydou's family also visited twice, seeing him for the first time in five years and witnessing just how "crazy" American college sport is.

There was a military flyover, fireworks and a cacophony of cowbells among the 60,000 crowd - a long-held tradition at Mississippi State.

With Seydou's college career now complete, it was time to enter the NFL Draft.

NFL teams recruit their best players through the draft, a three-day process that has become one of the biggest events in the NFL calendar.

Each year about 260 players are selected across seven rounds. They get a call from their new team and a few minutes later their name is announced on stage. A record 805,000 fans attended this year's draft in Pittsburgh.

Hundreds of prospects are evaluated by NFL experts and Seydou was projected to be picked on the final day, when rounds four to seven take place.

Former player Efe Obada was there to support the international hopefuls. Having also gone from London Warriors to the NFL, he is an academy ambassador and saw Traore at the try-outs in 2019.

So after the Miami Dolphins called Traore late in the fifth round, Obada "kind of hijacked" his announcement.

He ran into the office NFL commissioner Roger Goodell was using and told him "I wanna do it". Goodell agreed it "made sense" and they went on stage together to welcome Traore into the NFL.

"I thought it would be symbolic, passing on the torch," says Obada. "I've kind of gone through that journey and I wanted people to know that it's a moment. [Being drafted] doesn't just happen. This sport is about endurance and commitment."

As a former London Warriors coach, Aden Durde was aware of Traore's talent before he too attended the first academy try-outs.

And the British defensive co-ordinator, who helped the Seattle Seahawks win the Super Bowl in February, smiled when he heard Traore's name mentioned during this year's pre-draft process.

"It's so cool to see him go to different colleges and really kick down the door and break barriers," he says.

"That was the vision of the NFL Academy all those years ago. He's the first one and there's going to be plenty more. It's exciting times."

Travis Clayton was the first ex-academy player to be drafted but only spent a brief period with the programme in 2019 and did not attend a US college, so Traore is the first of its alumni to follow the full pathway.

Since the academy's inception more than 75 students have secured college football scholarships in the US.

Traore has remained cool, calm and collected throughout his journey, even when he strode on to the NFL Draft stage. Draped in a British flag, he stopped to put on a Dolphins cap and do his tea-sipping celebration for the camera.

But one day in June, far from the draft spotlight, his excitement got the better of him.

Zeinab says they used to joke about who would be the first to buy their mum a house. Seydou knew he had won when he signed a four-year rookie contract worth $4.8m (£3.6m).

And it was his older sister, not his mum, whom he called to say "I'm signing right now!"

Not all drafted players are guaranteed to play from the start of their rookie season. Teams must whittle their roster from 90 or 91 players down to 53 by 31 August.

Traore is trying to earn a spot during Miami's training camp but is backing himself to continue his remarkable journey in the NFL.

"It feels good [to be here]," he adds. "But I keep telling everyone, it's just the beginning."

title: Virginia university didn't know of student's conviction before campus shooting, report says
description: A Virginia university missed opportunities to learn of a student's terrorism-related conviction before the man opened fire in an ROTC class in March, injuring two students and killing an Army veteran ...
fullText:
RICHMOND, Va. (AP) — A Virginia university missed opportunities to learn of a student's terrorism-related conviction before the man opened fire in an ROTC class in March, injuring two students and killing an Army veteran who fought back with "extraordinary heroism," an investigative report released Tuesday found.

The federal probation officer working with Mohamed Bailor Jalloh, who spent eight years in prison for attempting to aid the Islamic State, did not share Jalloh's criminal background with Old Dominion University, despite the serious nature of the offense, according to the report, which was produced by the law firm Cooley on behalf of the university.

Jalloh, who also died in the March attack, had attended the public university in Norfolk beginning in 2007, was suspended in 2010 and reenrolled after his early release from prison in December 2024. He was readmitted to the school in May last year.

No federal or state law enforcement agency reported his prior conviction either, the report said.

State law prohibits the university from inquiring about student criminal history before admission or readmission, according to the report. The university could have asked readmitted students to voluntarily disclose their criminal history but did not at the time, the report said.

The university "had no knowledge of the risk Jalloh posed or his federal terrorism conviction," the report said. Had officials known, it's likely they would have sought his removal from campus, it said.

"Given that Virginia law requires universities to rely on student self-disclosure, it is even more important that other law enforcement agencies ensure that information that universities need to know to safeguard their students is shared with universities. This critical failure led to tragic consequences here," the report said.

Officials with the FBI, which the report said investigated Jalloh's original offense, didn't immediately respond to emailed requests for comment about the report's findings.

Paul Arnett, the chief U.S. probation officer for Virginia's eastern district federal court, reached briefly by phone, requested questions about the report's findings in writing, which the AP provided.

Jalloh, a former member of the Virginia National Guard, was sentenced to 11 years in prison after pleading guilty in 2017 to providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization, the Islamic State group, according to prison records. He completed a drug treatment program that allowed him early release from federal prison.

In March this year, Jalloh entered a classroom and asked whether it was an ROTC class. After students answered affirmatively, he opened fire, according to authorities and the report.

The university's president said the report also shed new light on the "extraordinary heroism and bravery" shown by the cadets and Lt. Col. Brandon Shah, the instructor who was killed.

Authorities and cadets who were in the room said they stabbed and disarmed Jalloh, the report said.

Shah "immediately grappled with the attacker, which allowed other brave students to come to his aid and many other students to escape unharmed," the report said.

Cadets tried to save Shah's life but he died at a hospital, the report said.

Family members of Shah could not immediately be reached for comment. An Old Dominion graduate and former Army pilot, he flew hundreds of hours on combat missions before returning to the university to lead the Army ROTC battalion, according to a biography published by the university.

While the report noted that the university's police department responded "almost immediately and effectively," it also recommended improvements to the university's safety and emergency response protocols.

"The campus community has my complete assurance that we will act quickly to fully implement Cooley's recommendations as we actively work to make our campus as safe and secure as possible," university President Brian O. Hemphill said in a statement.

fullText:
Salamanca City Central says it is pausing project with Realbotix as it addresses concerns including data privacy

A New York school district has walked back plans to introduce a humanoid robot at its high school after the proposal sparked backlash from educators and community members.

The Salamanca City Central school district announced on 24 July in a social media post that its pilot project with Toronto-based tech company Realbotix had been put on hold “while we work through enhanced student data privacy agreements with the New York State Education Department and continue engaging with our community and stakeholders”.

“Ensuring that appropriate privacy protections are in place and incorporating input from our community are important parts of the process. We appreciate your patience and will share additional updates as they become available,” added the school district, which is located on the Seneca Nation reservation in upstate New York and serves a large Native American population.

The reversal came after widespread criticism of the program, which would have brought a humanoid robot named Sally to Salamanca high school. According to a Realbotix press release issued in June, the approximately $58,000 robot with silicone skin and brown hair was intended to use “natural conversation, facial expressions and real-time interaction to create engaging, hands-on learning experiences”.

“The robot aims to encourage student participation and provide early exposure to emerging technologies,” the company also said.

A little more than two years before Friday’s announcement, Realbotix acquired Simulacra, a Las Vegas-based company that manufactures sex dolls.

The New York State United Teachers union had condemned the plans calling for high schoolers to be taught by a humanoid robot.

“A robot built by a company associated with sex dolls has no business in our classrooms,” Melinda Person, the union president, said in a 23 July statement.

Person added: “Our students don’t need robots. They need real relationships with caring adults. Educators notice when students are struggling, celebrate when they succeed and help them discover who they can become. No robot can do that, no matter how lifelike its skin or specific its regional accent.”

Lacey Pihlblad, the president of the Salamanca Teachers’ Association and a teacher at the high school, also criticized the proposal, saying: “The Salamanca teachers’ union as a whole is concerned about the background of the company of Realbotix. We’re very concerned about the security of the software that they’re implementing, and whether or not the data will be stored, how it will be gathered, [and] the recording capabilities.”

Other educators also questioned why the pilot program was being launched at a school serving a large Native American population.

Speaking to the Guardian recently, Sierra May Abrams, a substitute teacher at Salamanca high school, said: “Out of all the schools in New York state, let alone in the US, they chose to experiment on Native American children yet again.”

Abrams alluded to the history of brutality at Native American boarding schools in the US and said: “Our culture is struggling to stay alive due to the impact of [that] and what they did to our elders. We live on the only reservation located in a city so it’s just absolutely insane that we’re the ones ‘testing it out’.”

Following the Salamanca district’s decision to pause the program, Realbotix’s CEO, Andrew Kiguel, told New York Focus: “We fully respect any decision the school makes and encourage thorough due diligence by all parties involved.

“We want the program to be demonstrably safe, fully district-approved, and strongly supported by teachers … We stand firmly behind [the program] as a supportive tool designed to assist teachers and students, not replace them.”

After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.

He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and an address bearing the name of a woman associated with a French model casting agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” read one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”

Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”

More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”

As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”

About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.

On Monday, February 23, Bonnouvrier, the woman affiliated with the model casting agency, had sent an email to the principal of Redwood High School, calling Mueller’s post defamatory, demanding its immediate removal, and promising legal action if the school did not comply within 48 hours. And now the district superintendent was demanding that the Bark either redact Bonnouvrier’s name or delete the slide entirely.

title: The Chelsea-Man City link
description: Chelsea not only lost to Manchester City in the 2020 FA Youth Cup final, they also had a glimpse of their own future within the opposition ranks. fullText:
Chelsea not only lost to Manchester City in the 2020 FA Youth Cup final, they also had a glimpse of their own future within the opposition ranks.

So much so that Chelsea's first-team squad in the 2026-27 season could contain twice as many players who have graduated from City's academy as have come through their own system.

The latest addition is club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, who scored against the Blues' under-18s that night six years ago.

Fellow City academy graduate Cole Palmer was also on target in City's 3-2 victory at St George's Park, while Liam Delap led the line.

In addition, Xabi Alonso's squad features Romeo Lavia, Jamie Gittens and Tosin Adarabioyo - all of whom also came through City's youth system.

Together with Rogers, Palmer and Delap, the six players account for almost £300m in transfer fees paid by Chelsea since 2023.

Trevoh Chalobah also remains a Chelsea player, but he is in advanced talks over a move to Serie A side Como.

There are several reasons for Chelsea's interest in players developed from Manchester City, but one is the success of Palmer. Having moved between the clubs in 2023 for £40m plus £2.5m in add-ons, he has become one of the Premier League's standout performers.

One former insider told BBC Sport that anyone who comes from City "knows what good looks like".

Another factor is Joe Shields, who worked in City's academy recruitment department and is now involved in both youth and senior recruitment at Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea also employ a number of former City staff members, including first-team coach Calum McFarlane and recently promoted academy director Glenn van der Kraan.

There was also a brief spell for former City executive Tom Glick as Chelsea's president of business, while former Blues head coach Enzo Maresca and several members of his coaching staff previously worked at the Etihad.

Chelsea also held an interest in former City academy player Michael Olise before his move to Bayern Munich and previously explored a deal for defender Nico O'Reilly.

Judge Thomas Welsh KC told jurors it was a "distressing" case.

On one occasion he bit her when she refused to have intercourse with him or let him examine her mobile phone.

title: Appeals court reverses decision that freed pro-Palestinian Columbia activist Mohsen Mahdawi
description: A federal appeals panel has reversed a lower court decision ordering the release of pro-Palestinian activist Mohsen Mahdawi, opening the door to the re-arrest of a student protest organizer whom the T...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals panel has reversed a lower court decision ordering the release of pro-Palestinian activist Mohsen Mahdawi, opening the door to the re-arrest of a student protest organizer whom the Trump administration has spent more than a year trying to deport.

Tuesday's ruling from the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in New York overturns a previous decision by a federal judge in Vermont, which likened the government's efforts to expel him and other activists to McCarthyist repression.

In their unanimous decision, the panel found that the judge had overstepped his authority by intervening in Mahdawi's case before it had moved fully through the immigration court system.

The ruling mirrors a separate appellate panel's decision earlier this year against Mahmoud Khalil, a former classmate of Mahdawi's at Columbia University.

As with the ruling against Khalil, the appeals court did not weigh in on the merits of Mahdawi's claim that he was unconstitutionally targeted for criticizing Israel. He can seek a review from the federal courts over those claims once he has exhausted his options in the immigration courts, the panel wrote.

Mahdawi, 35, is currently appealing an order of removal issued against him by the Board of Immigration Appeals.

Attorneys for the American Civil Liberties Union, which represents Mahdawi, said Tuesday that the government could not detain or deport their client as the appeals process proceeds.

In a statement, Mahdawi called the appeals court decision "a grave setback," adding that it would hand the government "the power to intimidate, censor, and punish dissent without meaningful restraint."

An emailed inquiry to the Department of Homeland Security was not immediately returned.

Mahdawi was born in a refugee camp in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and became a legal permanent resident of the U.S. in 2015.

He was arrested by immigration agents during a citizenship interview in April 2025, part of the Trump administration's sweeping efforts to expel noncitizens who criticized Israel and protested against the war in Gaza. He was released two weeks later and graduated from Columbia soon after.

At a hearing in front of the 2nd Circuit last September, government attorneys argued against the release of both Mahdawi and another student, Rumeysa Ozturk, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University who was detained by masked federal agents after co-signing an op-ed critical of Israel.

Both students, the government said, had wrongly benefited from a form of relief, known as habeas corpus, that should be off-limits to those whose cases are moving through the immigration courts.

Attorneys for the students countered that there was little hope in seeking relief from an immigration court system overseen by President Donald Trump's Department of Justice.

The 2nd Circuit court is expected to issue a separate ruling concerning Ozturk's case.

title: 'A true great man, on and off the field' - your memories of Keegan
description: Mike: Our student flat was opposite the digs where Kevin Keegan lodged when he first arrived in Liverpool.  Mark: My first memory of football was Kevin Keegan scoring twice in the 1974 cup final against Newcastle.  Absolutely gutted when he left Liverpool.
fullText:
We asked for your memories of Liverpool legend Kevin Keegan after the sad news of his passing was announced on Monday.

Here are some of your replies and stories:

Mike: Our student flat was opposite the digs where Kevin Keegan lodged when he first arrived in Liverpool. He had a metallic green Ford Capri and I'd bump into him at the shops down the road (literally, as he only came up to my chin). Then on a Saturday we'd stand on the Kop and watch him dazzle - heady days!

Mark: My first memory of football was Kevin Keegan scoring twice in the 1974 cup final against Newcastle. Hooked from that day forward. Absolutely gutted when he left Liverpool.

John: A true Liverpool legend. Always gave 100% for club and country. He will be sorely missed.

Andrew: I met Kevin at Liverpool FC when he was visiting with Newcastle. I was working for Liverpool's sponsors at the time. He came briefly into the hospitality suite but was mobbed by all and quickly left. We followed him out as he made his way to the Newcastle team bus and had to push his way through a massive crowd of home supporters, all asking for his autograph. He ignored most of these requests. One supporter stopped him in his tracks with the comment: "Kevin please sign my programme, you're my hero… I even named my dog after you", he duly stopped and laughing signed the programme and climbed on board the coach. A true legend who will be sadly missed by all football supporters. RIP Kevin.

Rachel: Kevin Keegan was the reason I started supporting Liverpool from 1975 to the present date. He was always my number one player. A sad day.

Jamie: Mine is a childhood memory of Kevin Keegan training in his kit at his farm in North Wales. Used to see him regularly out practicing as I was too young at the time to go to Anfield. It's something I will never forget as the red kit stood out a mile.

Tim: My Dad is Greek and he meet Kevin Keegan in Athens in 1972 when Liverpool played AEK Athens in the Uefa Cup. Kevin stopped and asked my Dad for directions in Athens and he helped him and another player get where they wanted. Kevin said thanks and even got him a ticket for the game. A true great man, on and off the field.

Sam: In 2011 at 14-years-old, I won an EFL competition to be a pundit for a day. My pundit mentor was Kevin Keegan, a dream for any LFC fan. He never once judged my shoddy haircut or terrible jumper, and instead was a gentleman throughout the entire day, doing everything he could to encourage me and make the day magical. He will always be something pretty special to me.

title: Pamela Smart, serving life, seeks a new trial as a New Hampshire judge weighs her latest petition
description: Lawyers for Pamela Smart, who’s serving life in prison for orchestrating the murder of her husband by her teenage student in 1990, hope that a New Hampshire judge on Monday will allow her latest petit...
fullText:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — Lawyers for Pamela Smart, who's serving life in prison for orchestrating the murder of her husband by her teenage student in 1990, hope that a New Hampshire judge on Monday will allow her latest petition for a new trial to move forward.

Smart's trial was one of the first in the nation to be broadcast live on television from start to finish. She was a 22-year-old high school media coordinator when she began an affair with a 15-year-old boy who later fatally shot her husband, Gregory Smart, in Derry.

The shooter was freed in 2015 after serving a 25-year sentence. Though Smart denied knowledge of the plot, she was convicted of being an accomplice to first-degree murder and other crimes and was sentenced to life without parole.

Her petition for habeas corpus relief was filed in January. It seeks to overturn her conviction over what her lawyers claim were several constitutional violations.

Smart, 58, will be allowed to attend the hearing remotely from the Bedford Hills Correctional Facility for Women in New York.

Smart's lawyers argue that prosecutors misled the jury by providing them with inaccurate transcripts of surreptitiously recorded conversations of Smart that included words that were not audible on the recordings.

Among the words they claim weren't audible but in the transcript were the word "killed" in the sentence "you had your husband killed," the word "busted" in the sentence "I'm gonna be busted" and the word "murder" in the sentence "this would have been the perfect murder."

"Modern science confirms what common sense has always told us: when people are handed a script, they inevitably hear the words they are shown," Smart's attorney, Matthew Zernhelt, said in a statement earlier this year. "Jurors were not evaluating the recordings independently — they were being directed toward a conclusion, and that direction decided the verdict."

Smart's lawyers also argued that the verdict was tainted by the media attention and due to faulty instructions to the jury. They argued jurors were told they must find that Smart acted with premeditation, and were not told they must consider only evidence presented at trial.

They also argued the trial court gave her a mandatory life sentence without parole for being an accomplice to first-degree murder, despite New Hampshire not mandating that sentence for the charge.

Lawyers for the state asked the judge to dismiss the petition, saying nearly all of the claims are barred because they already were raised on appeal and resolved by the New Hampshire Supreme Court, or could have been raised on appeal with the court but were not.

They noted that during Smart's trial, the defense only expressed concern that the recording transcripts allegedly failed to account for the "doubling" of voices when two people speak at once. The judge instructed jurors that if the tapes differed from what they were reading, they should use what they heard, instead. The state Supreme Court noted that Smart's lawyers did not make any "particularized showing of inaccuracies in the transcripts relative to the recordings or how she may have been prejudiced" by them.

Smart's team hasn't proven other claims, such as ineffective assistance of counsel and having the case argued in New York, rather than in New Hampshire, the lawyers for the state said.

Smart's legal options are limited. She has unsuccessfully sought a sentence reduction hearing several times with an elected state council in New Hampshire that approves contracts and appointees to the courts and state agencies. She appealed one rejection to the state Supreme Court, which dismissed her petition in 2023.

Her latest petition was filed after New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte rejected her request last year to put the matter before the council again. Ayotte said she reviewed the case and decided it was not deserving of a hearing.

In 2024, Smart took full responsibility for her husband's death. She said in a video she spent years deflecting blame "almost as if it was a coping mechanism."

Smart's trial was a media circus and one of America's first high-profile cases about a sexual affair between a school employee and a student. The student, William Flynn, testified that Smart told him she needed her husband killed because she feared she would lose everything if they divorced and that she threatened to break up with him if he didn't kill her husband. Flynn and three other teens cooperated with prosecutors and all have since been released.

Flynn and 17-year-old Patrick Randall entered the Smarts' Derry condominium and forced Gregory Smart to his knees in the foyer. As Randall held a knife to the man's throat, Flynn fired a hollow-point bullet into his head. Both pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and were sentenced to 28 years to life. They were granted parole in 2015. Two other teenagers served prison sentences and have been released.

The case inspired Joyce Maynard's 1992 book "To Die For" and the 1995 film of the same name, starring Nicole Kidman and Joaquin Phoenix.

title: Anti-ICE walkout exposes how school district 'failed' parents, risked student safety: 'Broken my trust'
description: Internal emails and texts show Flagstaff Unified School District staff allegedly knew about the ICE protest days in advance and helped students walk out.
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: Internal emails, messages and memos from Arizona's Flagstaff Unified School District (FUSD) reveal that staff allegedly breached security protocol and violated several school policies by facilitating a student walkout to protest U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) earlier this year, according to America First Legal.

Hundreds of Flagstaff high school and middle school students walked out of class to protest ICE on Jan. 28. The protest came amid national controversy over the deaths of anti-ICE activists Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota. Immediately after the walkout, many parents, citing safety concerns, expressed outrage that they were not notified that their children had been allowed to leave school premises without their consent. One parent who said they had children under the age of 12 said the "district failed us as parents."

Documents obtained by America First Legal, a conservative watchdog group, reveal that FUSD officials knew about the walkout days in advance and also coordinated with students. The documents, which were reviewed by Fox News Digital, were obtained by America First Legal through a lawsuit forcing FUSD to comply with its public records request for records related to the walkout.

Screenshots from a district staff text group show faculty coordinating during the walkout. One staff member texted, "We have 75 plus students staged outside of fhs [Flagstaff High School] getting ready to walk." In the same message, the staff member wrote, "Looks like we have some members of the public joining."

Controversial Ice Tactic Actually Reduces Unintended 'Collateral' Arrests: Federal Agent

Another concerning text from a staff member read, "Be aware of propped open doors that are left for reentry."

In response to America First Legal's criticism, a spokesperson for the district told Fox News Digital that "We respectfully disagree that the Flagstaff Unified School District encouraged students to attend or intentionally ignored District policies."

The spokesperson said, "The District was placed in the challenging position of balancing students' First Amendment rights, student safety and school operations in the most appropriate way it could."

District policy dictates that "the Superintendent shall limit access to school buildings and grounds" and that faculty "maintain protocols regarding the distribution of keys or equipment to access District property." Further, FUSD policy also stipulates that students ages six to 16 are "required to attend school during the school's hours" and "the school in which the student is enrolled shall make a reasonable effort to promptly telephone and notify the parent/legal guardian or other person who has custody of the student of the student's absence from school."

An email from a student to then Flagstaff High School Principal Tadd Ragan shows that district staff was aware the protest would take place at least two days in advance. The student informed Ragan that students were planning to walk out of their classes to protest against ICE at 11:45 a.m. The student said the protest would occur "near a main road for more recognition" and asked for advice "in finding a more organized way of going about this."

In response, Ragan told the student that "as a District and School we have a plan to maintain a peaceful protest." In a subsequent email, Ragan asked the student, "Can you come by my office during first period?"

Another faculty member, Flagstaff "instructional coach" Janet Chavez-Vesely, sent an email to several school administrators the day before the protest, revealing that she had discussed the planned walkout with the student Hispanic Culture Club. Chavez-Vesely wrote that she "stayed neutral and answered questions while they planned."

Virginia School District Sued Over Alleged Policy Of Keeping Students' Gender Transitions Hidden From Parents

She noted that one of the students "plans to stop by and see me" to discuss the protest further. Chavez-Vesely told the school administrators, "I am available to support supervision," adding, "just let me know where."

Some parents who became aware of the walkout before it happened emailed the district, notifying staff that their children would be absent from school while citing safety concerns.

On Tuesday, one parent emailed Ragan, telling him, "I am keeping my daughter home from school this Wednesday as it has been brought to my attention that both Flagstaff high school and Coconino high school have planned out an entire protest."

The parent wrote, "This is not something that I want my child involved in nor do I want her around during it nor do I want her suffering any of the consequences that come with not participating and or being pressured into participating in potentially getting in a violent situation."

Another parent emailed faculty late on Tuesday night, writing, "My kids will not be at school tomorrow." The parent noted, "This is not something that I want my children exposed to or involved in as situations like this in the past have become violent and unsafe."

Meanwhile, at least one faculty member was excited about the protest, writing in a text, "This Walk out thing is going to be FUN!"

The morning of the protest, Sinagua Middle School Principal Christopher Koenker sent an email that FUSD "supports our students' constitutional rights to peaceful assembly and free expression and is aware of student-led events planned."

He wrote that "schools will neither encourage nor discourage student participation." He added that the district was looking into providing additional staff and law enforcement presence "for protection and supervision, not to suppress student expression."

After the protest, an internal "Walk Out Debrief" memo emphasized that "school isn't responsible for students' safety after they leave campus."

Another memo noted that one teacher, identified as "Ms. Donovan," took her class outside to witness "rights vs. responsibilities" on display at the walkout. An administrator noted that just three students remained inside and that "later conversations with the 3 students indicated that they really weren't comfortable being outside." The administrator noted she eventually asked Donovan to bring the class back inside "as it might appear that she was influencing them to be outside."

Laura Ingraham: Teaching Us History Has Become An Exercise In 'Self-loathing And Resentment'

In the same memo, the administrator noted that Donovan also discussed ICE operations in her class and had told students that officers had "used" a five-year-old "to lure the family out to take him." The administrator wrote that they had asked a student if she felt Donovan "pushes her opinions on her." The student answered that after the protest Donovan had asked students to raise their hands if they participated in the protest after which she "congratulated them," saying, "Great job for standing up for your first amendment rights."

Parents, however, quickly expressed that they felt outraged and blindsided.

One mother wrote that after learning of the protest, she and her husband "were terrified that our daughter was peer pressured (by friends, classmates, teachers, and the school district) to be a part of this."

"We're thankful that our daughter remained at school, due to fear and frustration, but there is still the 'what if'? What if something happened to any students during the walkout?" she continued, adding, "We expect the district to be transparent and not jeopardize our children's safety."

Another middle school parent wrote that they were not made aware of the protest or contacted until the end of the day. They wrote that their child "was under the impression this was a school sponsored event," given that faculty allegedly provided "maps" and directions to the event.

"This school district has broken my trust and neglected your responsibilities and disregard for your own policies," the parent wrote.

Commenting on this, America First Legal Senior Counsel James Rogers told Fox News Digital that "What these documents show is a stunning betrayal of that trust."

Rogers said that FUSD's "conduct raises serious questions about whether district employees crossed that line."

"Parents deserved to know where their children were. The law required these officials to act, and they failed on both counts," he said.

fullText:
Jul. 18—When a door closes, another may open.

That's exactly what happened for 2019 Grangeville High School graduate Chase Adkison when he signed with the reigning World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers' organization in June.

Following a long-term injury to Dodgers All-Star catcher Will Smith, L.A. initiated a chain reaction of catcher promotions and signings, eventually finding Adkison, recently released by the St. Louis Cardinals' organization.

Adkison reported to the Dodgers' High-A affiliate, the Great Lakes Loons in Midland, Mich, where through 13 games he has nine hits, five walks, a double, four RBI and nine runs.

In parts of four seasons in minor league baseball, Adkison is batting .268, with five home runs, 55 RBI and 56 runs.

The Grangeville grad found his way to professional baseball by way of the now-defunct Boise State baseball program in 2020, San Jacinto College (Texas) in 2021 and two standout seasons at Oklahoma State, where he started 98 total games and batted .282, with 11 home runs, 16 doubles, a triple, 41 walks, 69 RBI and 77 runs.

"This move is another opportunity to continue playing professional baseball," Adkison said in an Idaho County Free Press article. "I'm excited to be wearing a new uniform and have the chance to compete every day. I'm grateful for the opportunity and looking forward to helping the organization however I can."

Adkison holds four Grangeville High baseball records seven years after his career concluded, including single-season batting average (.653), single-season triples (eight), career hits (151) and career triples (20), according to the Idaho County Free Press.

Here's a look at other local connections to major and minor league baseball in 2026, including 10 Washington State Cougars and four Lewis-Clark State Warriors.

Connor Brogdon — RHP — Cleveland Guardians

With the Angels last season, Connor Brogdon signed in December with the Cleveland Guardians.

In 15 appearances, Brogdon has turned in a 2-2 record and 5.28 ERA. He has struck out 14 through 15 1/3 innings.

Seth Brown — OF — New York Yankees — Triple-A

Weeks before shuttling off to Florida for spring training, MLB veteran Seth Brown visited his alma mater Lewis-Clark State for a first-of-its-kind fundraising dinner.

The favor benefited his college coach, Jeremiah Robbins, who returned to LCSC this past season.

Brown spoke about how his time in Lewiston springboarded him to the career he has had. After seven years with the Athletics, Brown signed with the New York Yankees this past winter and is waiting for his opportunity.

With the Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders, Brown has logged 53 games and is batting .235, with 43 hits, including six doubles, a triple and nine home runs en route to 21 RBI and 23 runs.

Drake George — RHP — San Francisco Giants — Single-A

After turning in a 3.20 ERA in Year 1, Drake George has been on the Giants org's injured list for the entire season so far.

Last year, George struck out 62 through 56 1/3 innings pitched.

Jadon Williamson — RHP — Miami Marlins — FCL Marlins

The most recent Warrior-turned-pro-baseball player on this list, Jadon Williamson has gotten two starts and made 11 total appearances for the Florida Complex League Marlins in 2026 after being selected in the 11th round of the 2025 MLB draft.

Williamson holds a 15.66 ERA, but he has struck out 24 batters through 16 2/3 innings pitched.

Kyle Manzardo — 1B/DH — Cleveland Guardians

WSU's former star slugger Kyle Manzardo has had a so-so year at the plate in 2026, but what transpired in his life over a year ago dwarfs any sort of success or failure he could experience between the lines.

In July 2025, Manzardo's mother, Windy Manzardo, underwent long-awaited heart transplant surgery. Kyle Manzardo flew from Houston, where the Cleveland Guardians had just arrived, to Spokane to be with his mother.

The surgery was a success, and since then, Windy and Kyle's father, Paul Manzardo, have gotten to watch their son live without the cloud of Windy's condition hanging over their lives.

"I guess now that it's over, I've kind of realized how heavy that was to just be carrying it around with you for a couple of years now," Kyle Manzardo said via MLB.com. "Just grateful it's hopefully done with now."

At the All-Star break, Manzardo was batting .215 through 87 games with seven doubles, one triple, 10 home runs and 30 RBI along with 32 runs scored for the 51-46 Cleveland Guardians, a half a game back from the Chicago White Sox in the American League Central division as of Friday.

Ryan Walker — RHP — San Francisco Giants

Ian Hamilton — RHP — Atlanta Braves — Triple-A

Ian Hamilton spent the last three years in the big leagues with the New York Yankees. He signed with the Atlanta Braves' org in the offseason and, in four big-league appearances with the Braves, allowed four earned runs on six hits.

Brandon White — RHP — Miami Marlins — Triple-A

From Chehalis, Wash., Brandon White has been working his way up the Miami Marlins' farm system ranks since the club drafted him out of WSU in 2021.

This year with the Triple-A Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp, White has pitched 71 2/3 innings with 16 appearances and 14 starts. He has struck out 87 batters and posted a 4.40 ERA.

Jonah Advincula — OF — Cleveland Guardians — Double-A

After starting the season injured, Jonah Advincula has joined Double-A Akron for nine games, going 9-for-28 at the plate with three doubles, three home runs, four stolen bases and 10 runs scored.

Sam Brown — INF — Washington Nationals — Double-A

Acquired by the Nationals as part of a July 30, 2025, trade with the Angels, Brown is hitting .238 with 49 hits through 56 games. He has 11 doubles, three home runs, 17 RBI and 19 runs.

Zane Mills — RHP — Chicago Cubs — Double-A

Before suffering a season-ending knee injury, Zane Mills made one appearance for Double-A Knoxville in the Chicago Cubs' organization.

Dakota Hawkins — RHP — New York Mets — High-A

Dakota Hawkins made one appearance each in the Double-A and Triple-A levels of the New York Mets' org, but has settled in with High-A Brooklyn, where through 17 appearances he is 3-0 with two holds, a 2.54 ERA and 33 strikeouts.

Will Cresswell — C — Toronto Blue Jays — Single-A

Cresswells's last 12 months have been eventful. The WSU's most-recent pro wrapped up the 2025 season in Pullman and was drafted by the Toronto Blue Jays in July 2025. He spent March representing Great Britain in the World Baseball Classic.

With the Blue Jays' Single-A affiliate, Creswell has played in 34 games and notched 23 hits, including three doubles, a home run along with 15 RBI and 11 runs.

Connor Wilford — RHP — Seattle Mariners — ACL

Connor Wilford started the year with Lexington of the Atlantic League, an independent baseball league, before the Seattle Mariners purchased his contract. While not associated with an MLB organization, left-handed pitcher A.J. Block and catcher Jacob Morrow play in independent leagues. Block hurls for a Lake County (Wis.) team, while Morrow plays for a Lincoln (Neb.) squad.

Block was with the Angels' Double-A affiliate last season and pitched 14 games for Durango in the Mexican League, recording 14 strikeouts through 8 2/3 innings.
